title: Tree Node
statement:
One table stores a rooted tree:

- `Tree(id, p_id)`: one row per node; `id` is unique. `p_id` is the id of the node's parent, or `null` for the root. The rows always form one valid tree: exactly one root, every `p_id` names a node in the table, and there are no cycles.

Label every node with its kind:

- `'Root'` when it has no parent (`p_id` is `null`), even if it also has children;
- `'Inner'` when it has a parent and at least one child;
- `'Leaf'` when it has a parent and no children.

Return the columns `id` and `type`, one row per node, in any order.
constraints: Exactly one node has p_id = null (the root)
Every non-null p_id is the id of a node in Tree
The parent links contain no cycles
reference:
WITH parents AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT p_id AS id
  FROM Tree
  WHERE p_id IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT t.id,
  CASE
    WHEN t.p_id IS NULL THEN 'Root'
    WHEN t.id IN (SELECT id FROM parents) THEN 'Inner'
    ELSE 'Leaf'
  END AS type
FROM Tree AS t;
brute:
SELECT id, 'Root' AS type
FROM Tree
WHERE p_id IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT t.id, 'Inner'
FROM Tree AS t
WHERE t.p_id IS NOT NULL
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Tree AS c WHERE c.p_id = t.id)
UNION ALL
SELECT t.id, 'Leaf'
FROM Tree AS t
WHERE t.p_id IS NOT NULL
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Tree AS c WHERE c.p_id = t.id)
notes:
## Intuition

A node's kind depends on two facts: does it have a parent, and does any node name it as a parent. The first is visible in the node's own row (`p_id IS NULL`). The second needs the set of ids that appear in the `p_id` column. With that set, a `CASE` expression checks the conditions in priority order: the root first, because a root with children would otherwise look inner.

## Approach

1. CTE `parents`: the distinct non-null `p_id` values, i.e. every node that has at least one child.
2. Scan `Tree` (alias `t`) and build `type` with `CASE`:
   - `p_id IS NULL` → `'Root'`;
   - otherwise, `id` is in `parents` → `'Inner'`;
   - otherwise → `'Leaf'`.

## Example 1, step by step

- `parents` holds the `p_id` values 1 and 2 (node 1 is the parent of 2 and 3, node 2 the parent of 4 and 5).
- Node 1 has `p_id = null`, so it is `Root`; the first branch wins even though 1 is also in `parents`.
- Node 2 has a parent and is in `parents`: `Inner`.
- Nodes 3, 4 and 5 have parents and are not in `parents`: `Leaf`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for n nodes to build `parents` and probe it (O(n) with hashing).
- Space: O(n) for `parents`.

## Pitfalls

- Testing "has children" before "has no parent" labels a root with children as `Inner`; branch order matters in `CASE`.
- `id NOT IN (SELECT p_id FROM Tree)` is never true, because that list contains the root's `null`; drop the nulls (as `parents` does) or use `NOT EXISTS`.
- An inner join from a node to its children drops leaves, and without `DISTINCT` a node with several children can be reported more than once.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `parents` | ids of nodes that have at least one child |
| `t` | `Tree`, one output row per node |
| `CASE ... END AS type` | `'Root'`, `'Inner'` or `'Leaf'`, checked in that order |

narration.1: The CTE collects every node that is somebody's parent.
narration.2: DISTINCT keeps one row per parent, however many children it has.
narration.4: The root's null p_id is dropped so the list holds only real node ids.
narration.6: Every node in Tree produces exactly one output row with its id.
narration.8: A node without a parent is the root; this branch comes first so a root with children is not called inner.
narration.9: A node with a parent that also appears in the parents list has children, so it is inner.
narration.10: Everything else has a parent but no children: a leaf.
narration.11: The CASE result is named type, the required output column.
